heading: Velocity and distance
text: Differentiation recovers velocity from a distance function, while integration recovers the change in distance from velocity. Geometrically, velocity is the slope of the distance graph and change in distance is signed area under the velocity graph.
formulas: change in f = signed area under v

heading: Constant velocity
text: For constant velocity, distance is a linear function of time. The initial distance changes the intercept but not the slope.

heading: Forward and backward motion
text: If a car moves forward at velocity V for time T and then backward at velocity -V for the same time, its final displacement is zero. The positive and negative rectangular areas under the velocity graph cancel.

heading: Functions, domain, and range
text: A function assigns one output to each input in its domain. The domain is the allowed set of inputs and the range is the set of resulting outputs. A distance function can be continuous while its velocity changes by jumps.

heading: Slope in a break-even model
text: For a linear cost and linear income model, break-even occurs where the two functions are equal. Comparing their slopes determines whether income can eventually catch cost.

heading: Differences and sums
text: For values sampled at equally spaced times, a discrete velocity is the difference between consecutive distances. Adding all consecutive differences recovers the total change in distance because the intermediate terms cancel.

heading: Piecewise linear calculus
text: On each linear segment, velocity is the constant slope of the distance graph. Conversely, the signed area under a piecewise constant velocity graph gives the change in distance over the interval.

heading: Composition multiplies slopes
text: For the linear functions g(t) = 2t + 1 and f(t) = 4t, composing f after g gives f(g(t)) = 8t + 4. Its slope 8 is the product of the slopes 4 and 2.

heading: Step functions and concentrated change
text: A short burst of large velocity can produce a fixed change in distance. As the burst becomes narrower and taller while its area stays fixed, the distance approaches a step and the velocity approaches an impulse-like delta function.

heading: Recovering distance from two constant speeds
text: If velocity is 2 until t = 5 and 3 afterward, with f(0) = 0, continuity fixes the second linear piece. At t = 5 the distance is 10, so afterward f(t) = 10 + 3(t - 5).

heading: Average velocity
text: Average velocity over an interval is change in distance divided by change in time. On the graph of distance, it is the slope of the secant line joining the two endpoints.

heading: Instantaneous velocity
text: Instantaneous velocity is the limiting value of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero. Geometrically, secant lines approach the tangent line and their slopes approach the derivative.

heading: Velocity for f(t) = t^2
text: For f(t) = t^2, the average velocity from t to t + h simplifies to 2t + h. Letting h approach zero gives the instantaneous velocity v(t) = 2t.

heading: Constant acceleration
text: Under constant acceleration a, velocity is linear and distance is quadratic. The constant b is initial velocity and c is initial distance.

heading: Local slope and accumulated area
text: Slope is local: velocity at one instant depends on the distance graph near that instant. Accumulated distance is global: finding area up to a time requires the earlier velocity history and an initial distance.
formulas: v(t) depends on f near t
f(t) = f(0) + accumulated area under v

heading: Position on the unit circle
text: A ball moves counterclockwise around the unit circle at constant speed, with its angle equal to the time t measured in radians. Its coordinates are x = cos t and y = sin t, so the position is completely described by the sine and cosine of t.

heading: Radian measure
text: An angle in radians is the arc length it cuts off on a circle of radius one. A full turn is 2*pi radians, which equals 360 degrees, so the ball completes the circle at time t = 2*pi rather than t = 360.

heading: Velocity around the circle
text: The velocity vector is tangent to the circle, perpendicular to the radius, and has length equal to the speed. For unit speed the components are the derivatives of position: the horizontal velocity is -sin t and the vertical velocity is cos t.
formulas: velocity is tangent, perpendicular to the radius

heading: Harmonic motion of the shadow
text: The shadow of the ball on the vertical axis performs simple harmonic motion. Its height f(t) = sin t oscillates between -1 and 1, stopping at the top and bottom and moving fastest through the center, so its speed is not constant even though the ball's speed is.
formulas: speed = 0 at top and bottom, 1 at the center

heading: Slope of the sine is the cosine
text: The upward velocity of the mass equals the upward velocity of the ball, which is cos t. So when distance is sin t the velocity is cos t: the slope of the sine curve is the cosine. By the same reasoning the slope of the cosine curve is minus the sine.
formulas: slope of sin t = cos t

heading: Going around twice as fast
text: If the ball reaches angle 2t at time t, its position is x = cos 2t and y = sin 2t, so a full circle now takes only t = pi. The velocity components double to -2 sin 2t and 2 cos 2t, giving speed 2.

heading: The six trigonometric ratios
text: In a right triangle with near side x, opposite side y, and hypotenuse r, the six functions are the ratios of these sides. They do not change when the triangle is scaled, and the reciprocal functions come directly from the first three.

heading: Angles on a circle in radians
text: Moving from triangles to a circle lets angles exceed 90 degrees. Angles are measured counterclockwise from the positive x axis, and the radian measure of an angle is the arc length on a unit circle, so 180 degrees is pi radians.

heading: Even, odd, and periodic
text: Reversing the sign of the angle keeps x and r but flips y. Therefore cosine is even while sine and tangent are odd. Adding a full turn of 2*pi changes nothing, so all six functions are periodic with period 2*pi (tangent repeats every pi).

heading: Pythagorean and addition identities
text: The Pythagorean identity follows from x^2 + y^2 = r^2. The addition formulas express the sine and cosine of a sum, and setting the two angles equal gives the double-angle formulas used later to find slopes.
formulas: sin(x+y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos(x+y) = cos x cos y - sin x sin y

heading: Evaluating the functions at 2*pi/3
text: At the angle 2*pi/3 (that is, 120 degrees) the point on the unit circle has x = -1/2 and y = sqrt(3)/2. The six ratios follow directly, with the tangent negative because x is negative while y is positive.

heading: Plotting sin n at whole numbers
text: The continuous curve y = sin x is smooth, but plotting y = sin n only at the integers n samples that curve. The sampled points surprisingly appear to line up along many separate sine curves, an effect that comes from how the sampling interacts with the period 2*pi.
formulas: y = sin n for integer n
sin x is continuous; sin n samples it

heading: Why points fall near zero
text: A point sits near zero exactly when the integer n is close to a multiple of pi. Because 22/7 is close to pi, sin 22 is only about 0.01, and 44 is close to 14*pi so sin 44 is about 0.02. These near-multiples of pi start the visible sampled curves.

heading: Aliasing, scale, and Moire patterns
text: The sampled points form about 44 apparent sine curves, and what the eye sees depends entirely on scale: tilting or compressing the axis reveals different patterns. The hexagons in the denser plot are a Moire pattern caused by interference between periodic patterns.

heading: The derivative as a limit
text: The derivative of a function f at a point x is the limit of the average rate of change over a shrinking interval h. It measures the instantaneous rate at which f changes and equals the slope of the graph at that point.

heading: Notation and the difference quotient
text: The same derivative is written f'(x), df/dx, or the limit of delta f over delta x. The difference quotient delta f / delta x is the slope of a secant line, and its limit is the slope of the tangent line.
formulas: df/dx = lim_(Delta x->0) Delta f/Delta x
Delta f = f(x + Delta x) - f(x)

heading: Derivative of x squared
text: For f(x) = x^2 the difference quotient simplifies to 2x + h. Letting h approach zero gives the derivative 2x, so the slope of the parabola grows linearly with x.

heading: Derivative of one over x
text: For f(x) = 1/x the difference quotient becomes -1/(x(x+h)). As h approaches zero this tends to -1/x^2, which is negative because the graph of 1/x is always falling.

heading: The power rule
text: The derivative of a power x to the n is n times x to the n minus one. This rule holds for every constant exponent and is the workhorse for differentiating polynomials.

heading: Sum and constant-multiple rules
text: Differentiation is linear: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor pulls straight through. This lets any polynomial be differentiated term by term.
formulas: d/dx (a x^2 + b x + c) = 2a x + b

heading: Differentiating a polynomial
text: Applying the power rule to each term of f(x) = 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 4x - 7 gives the derivative term by term. The constant term contributes nothing to the slope.

heading: Negative and fractional powers
text: The power rule extends to negative and fractional exponents, so reciprocals and roots can be differentiated the same way after rewriting them as powers of x.

heading: The tangent line
text: The tangent line to a graph at a point has slope equal to the derivative there. It is the line that best matches the curve near the point of contact.

heading: Equation of the tangent
text: Given the point of contact and the derivative, the tangent line is written in point-slope form. This linear function is later used as the linear approximation of f near a.

heading: Tangent to a parabola
text: For f(x) = x^2 at x = 3 the slope is f'(3) = 6 and the point is (3, 9). The tangent line is therefore y = 9 + 6(x - 3), or y = 6x - 9.

heading: From secant to tangent
text: A secant line joins two points on the curve; as the second point slides toward the first, the secant slopes approach the tangent slope. This limiting process is exactly the definition of the derivative.

heading: Derivatives of sine and cosine
text: The derivative of the sine is the cosine, and the derivative of the cosine is minus the sine. These follow from circular motion and from the small-angle limits below.

heading: The key small-angle limits
text: The derivative formulas rest on two limits as the angle goes to zero: sin h over h approaches one, and (1 - cos h) over h approaches zero. They express that for small angles the sine is nearly the angle itself.

heading: Deriving the slope of sine
text: Expanding sin(x+h) with the addition formula and dividing by h separates into cos x times (sin h / h) plus sin x times ((cos h - 1)/h). Taking the limit gives cos x.
formulas: sin(x+h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h

heading: The product rule
text: The derivative of a product is the first times the derivative of the second plus the second times the derivative of the first. It is not simply the product of the derivatives.
formulas: (x^2 sin x)' = 2x sin x + x^2 cos x

heading: The quotient rule
text: The derivative of a quotient has the denominator times the derivative of the numerator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator, all divided by the denominator squared.

heading: The power rule from products
text: Repeating the product rule shows that the power rule holds for any integer exponent, including negative ones obtained through the quotient rule.

heading: Applying the product rule
text: For y = x^3 cos x the product rule gives 3x^2 cos x plus x^3 times the derivative of cosine, which is minus sine. Combining the terms gives the derivative.
formulas: y' = 3x^2 cos x - x^3 sin x

heading: The limit of a function
text: A function has limit L as x approaches a if the values f(x) stay arbitrarily close to L whenever x is close enough to a. The limit does not depend on the value, or even existence, of f at a itself.
formulas: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0

heading: Limit laws
text: Limits respect sums, products, and quotients as long as the denominator limit is not zero. These laws let complicated limits be computed from simple pieces.
formulas: lim (f + g) = lim f + lim g
lim (f/g) = lim f / lim g if lim g != 0

heading: A zero-over-zero limit
text: The limit of (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) as x approaches 1 looks like 0/0, but factoring cancels x - 1 and leaves x + 1, whose limit is 2.

heading: Continuous functions
text: A function is continuous at a point when its limit there exists and equals the function value. Continuity means the graph has no jumps, holes, or breaks at that point.
formulas: no jump, hole, or break at a

heading: Differentiable implies continuous
text: If a function has a derivative at a point it must be continuous there, but the converse fails: a continuous function can have a corner where no derivative exists.
formulas: differentiable at a => continuous at a
|x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0

heading: The Intermediate Value Theorem
text: A function continuous on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values. In particular, if it changes sign it must cross zero somewhere in the interval.
formulas: f takes every value between f(a) and f(b)

heading: Linear approximation
text: Near a point a, a smooth function is closely matched by its tangent line. Replacing the curve by this line gives the linear approximation, accurate for small changes in x.
formulas: Delta f approximately f'(a) Delta x

heading: Differentials
text: The differential dy is the change along the tangent line for an input change dx. It estimates the true change delta y and becomes exact in the limit of small dx.
formulas: dy approximately Delta y for small dx

heading: Approximating a square root
text: To estimate sqrt(4.1), use a = 4 where the value and slope are known. The linear approximation gives 2 + (1/4)(0.1) = 2.025, very close to the true value.

heading: Critical points
text: A maximum or minimum of a differentiable function occurs where the derivative is zero. These critical points, together with the endpoints, are the only candidates for extreme values.
formulas: f'(x) = 0 at an interior maximum or minimum

heading: First and second derivative tests
text: At a critical point, a positive second derivative signals a local minimum and a negative one a local maximum. Alternatively, a sign change of the first derivative from plus to minus marks a maximum.

heading: Largest area for fixed perimeter
text: A rectangle with fixed perimeter P has area A(x) = x(P/2 - x). Setting the derivative to zero gives x = P/4, so the maximum-area rectangle is a square.

heading: The second derivative
text: The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative. In motion it is the acceleration, the rate at which velocity changes.

heading: Concavity and bending
text: Where the second derivative is positive the graph bends upward (concave up); where it is negative the graph bends downward. A point where concavity changes is an inflection point.

heading: Position, velocity, acceleration
text: For f(t) = (1/2) a t^2 the velocity is a t and the acceleration is the constant a. The parabola is concave up when a is positive.

heading: Reading a graph from its derivatives
text: The sign of the first derivative tells where a function rises or falls, and the sign of the second derivative tells how it bends. Together they locate maxima, minima, and inflection points for sketching.

heading: Asymptotes
text: A vertical asymptote appears where the function blows up as x approaches a finite value, and a horizontal asymptote appears where the function levels off as x goes to infinity.
formulas: vertical: f(x) -> infinity as x -> a
horizontal: f(x) -> L as x -> infinity

heading: Sketching a cubic
text: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x the derivative 3x^2 - 3 vanishes at x = plus or minus 1, giving a local maximum at -1 and a local minimum at 1. The second derivative 6x makes it concave down then up, with an inflection at 0.

heading: The conic sections
text: Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas are the curves cut from a cone and are described by second-degree equations in x and y. Each has a standard equation revealing its shape.

heading: Focus and directrix
text: A parabola is the set of points equally far from a focus and a directrix line. An ellipse keeps the sum of distances to two foci constant, and a hyperbola keeps the difference constant.
formulas: parabola: distance to focus = distance to directrix

heading: Slope on a parabola
text: For the parabola y = x^2 the slope is 2x, so the tangent steepens away from the vertex. This links the conic's geometry to the derivative.

heading: Iteration and fixed points
text: An iteration repeatedly applies a function, feeding each output back as the next input. A fixed point is a value left unchanged by the function, where the sequence can settle.

heading: When iteration converges
text: Near a fixed point the iteration converges when the size of the derivative of F is less than one, and diverges when it is greater than one. The derivative controls whether errors shrink or grow.

heading: Iterating the cosine
text: Repeatedly taking the cosine of any starting angle converges to about 0.739, the solution of x = cos x. The iteration works because the slope of cosine stays below one there.

heading: Newton's method
text: Newton's method finds a root by following the tangent line to where it crosses zero, then repeating. Each step subtracts f divided by f prime from the current guess.
formulas: tangent hits zero at the next guess

heading: Fast convergence and chaos
text: Near a simple root Newton's method roughly doubles the number of correct digits each step. Far from a root, or near points where the derivative vanishes, the iteration can behave chaotically.

heading: Newton's method for a square root
text: To solve x^2 = a, Newton's method becomes averaging x with a/x. Starting from a rough guess, a few steps give an accurate square root of a.

heading: The Mean Value Theorem
text: For a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable inside, there is a point where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope across the interval. Somewhere the tangent is parallel to the secant.

heading: l'Hopital's rule
text: When a limit gives the indeterminate form 0/0 or infinity over infinity, it equals the limit of the ratio of the derivatives, provided that limit exists.
formulas: lim f/g = lim f'/g' when 0/0 or infinity/infinity

heading: Applying l'Hopital
text: The limit of (sin x)/x as x approaches 0 is 0/0. Differentiating top and bottom gives (cos x)/1, whose limit at 0 is 1.
formulas: lim_(x->0) sin x / x = lim_(x->0) cos x / 1 = 1

heading: The chain rule
text: To differentiate a composition, multiply the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function by the derivative of the inner function. Rates of change multiply along the chain.

heading: Differentiating sin of x squared
text: For y = sin(x^2), the outer derivative is cos(x^2) and the inner derivative is 2x. Multiplying gives 2x cos(x^2).

heading: A power of a function
text: For y = (1 + x^2)^5 the outer power rule gives 5(1 + x^2)^4 and the inner derivative is 2x. The product is the chain-rule derivative.

heading: Implicit differentiation
text: When y is defined implicitly by an equation, differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function and using the chain rule, then solve for dy/dx.

heading: Slope on a circle
text: Differentiating x^2 + y^2 = 25 gives 2x + 2y (dy/dx) = 0, so the slope is -x/y. The tangent is horizontal at the top and vertical at the sides.

heading: Related rates
text: Related-rates problems link the time derivatives of quantities tied by an equation. Differentiating the relation with respect to time connects the known rate to the unknown one.
formulas: if A = pi r^2 then dA/dt = 2 pi r (dr/dt)

heading: Inverse functions
text: An inverse function undoes the original, sending each output back to its input. It exists when the function is one-to-one, and its graph is the reflection across the line y = x.

heading: Derivative of an inverse
text: The slope of the inverse is the reciprocal of the slope of the original at the corresponding point. Reflecting the graph turns rise over run into run over rise.

heading: Derivative of the cube root
text: Since the cube root inverts x^3, whose derivative is 3x^2, the derivative of the cube root of y is one over 3 times y to the two-thirds power.

heading: Derivatives of arcsine and arccosine
text: Inverting sine and cosine gives functions whose derivatives are algebraic. The derivative of arcsine is one over the square root of one minus x squared; arccosine is its negative.

heading: Derivative of arctangent
text: The inverse tangent has the especially clean derivative one over one plus x squared, which appears often in integration.

heading: Arctangent with the chain rule
text: For y = arctan(3x) the outer derivative is one over one plus (3x) squared, and the inner derivative is 3, giving 3 over one plus nine x squared.

heading: The idea of the integral
text: The integral adds up many small pieces to measure a whole, such as the area under a curve. It reverses the derivative: from velocity it recovers distance by accumulating change.
formulas: integral adds pieces v * Delta t

heading: Sums approximate area
text: Rectangles of width delta x and height f approximate the area under a curve. As the widths shrink, the sum of rectangle areas approaches the exact integral.
formulas: area approximately sum of f(x_i) Delta x
exact area = limit as Delta x -> 0

heading: Area under a line
text: The area under v = t from 0 to T is a triangle with base T and height T, giving (1/2) T^2. This matches the distance from constant acceleration.
formulas: area under v = t from 0 to T

heading: Antiderivatives
text: An antiderivative of f is a function whose derivative is f. Any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, so the general antiderivative includes an added constant C.

heading: Antiderivative of a power
text: Reversing the power rule, the antiderivative of x to the n is x to the n plus one over n plus one, valid whenever n is not minus one.

heading: Finding an antiderivative
text: The antiderivative of 3x^2 + 2 is x^3 + 2x plus a constant, because differentiating that returns the original function.

heading: Summation versus integration
text: Sums add discrete terms while integrals add continuous pieces. A finite sum with many small terms approaches the integral, so integration is the continuous limit of summation.
formulas: sum of f(i) Delta x -> integral of f dx

heading: Closed forms for sums
text: The sum of the first n integers and of the first n squares have closed forms. Dividing by powers of n and letting n grow recovers the corresponding integrals.

heading: Area of a parabola by sums
text: Summing rectangles under y = x^2 from 0 to 1 uses the sum of squares. As the number of rectangles grows the total approaches one third, the value of the integral.

heading: Integration by substitution
text: Substitution reverses the chain rule: replacing an inner function by u and dx by du over the inner derivative turns a hard integral into a simple one.
formulas: integral f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = integral f(u) du

heading: A substitution example
text: For the integral of 2x times cos(x^2), let u = x^2 so du = 2x dx. The integral becomes the integral of cos u, which is sin u, giving sin(x^2) plus a constant.

heading: The definite integral
text: The definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums over an interval and equals the signed area between the graph and the axis. Area below the axis counts as negative.
formulas: integral_a^b f(x) dx = lim sum f(x_i) Delta x
signed area between curve and axis

heading: Limits and orientation
text: Swapping the limits of integration changes the sign, and an integral over a zero-width interval is zero. Splitting the interval adds the integrals over the parts.

heading: Evaluating a definite integral
text: The integral of x from 0 to 2 is the area of a triangle, giving 2. This matches the antiderivative x^2 over 2 evaluated at the endpoints.

heading: Properties of the integral
text: The integral is linear and respects order: constants factor out, sums split apart, and a larger integrand gives a larger integral over the same interval.
formulas: integral (a f + b g) = a integral f + b integral g
if f <= g then integral f <= integral g

heading: Average value of a function
text: The average value of a function on an interval is its integral divided by the length of the interval. The Mean Value Theorem for integrals says the function actually attains this average somewhere.
formulas: f(c) = average for some c in (a, b)

heading: Average of x squared
text: The average value of x^2 on the interval from 0 to 1 is the integral one third divided by the length one, so the average is one third.

heading: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
text: The Fundamental Theorem links derivatives and integrals: a definite integral equals the change in an antiderivative, and differentiating an integral with variable upper limit returns the integrand.

heading: Why the two parts fit together
text: Accumulating a rate and then taking its derivative are inverse operations. This is why finding areas reduces to finding antiderivatives instead of computing limits of sums.

heading: Using the theorem
text: The integral of cos x from 0 to pi over 2 equals sin evaluated at the endpoints, which is one minus zero, so the answer is one.

heading: The trapezoidal rule
text: When an antiderivative is unavailable, numerical rules estimate the integral. The trapezoidal rule replaces the curve by straight segments and averages the endpoint heights on each strip.

heading: Simpson's rule
text: Simpson's rule fits parabolas through pairs of strips, giving far greater accuracy than trapezoids. Its error shrinks like the fourth power of the strip width.

heading: Estimating an integral numerically
text: To estimate the integral of 1 over x from 1 to 2, sampling the height at several points and applying the trapezoidal rule gives a value close to the true natural logarithm of 2.

heading: Exponentials and logarithms overview
text: Exponential functions grow at a rate proportional to their size, and logarithms are their inverses. This pairing describes growth, decay, and any process where change scales with the current amount.
formulas: log_b is the inverse of b^x

heading: Laws of exponents and logarithms
text: Multiplying powers adds exponents, and the logarithm turns products into sums. These mirror-image rules make exponentials and logarithms inverse operations.

heading: The natural exponential
text: The number e is the base for which the exponential is its own derivative. This is what makes e^x the natural choice throughout calculus.

heading: Derivative of a general exponential
text: Any exponential differentiates to itself times a constant, the natural logarithm of the base. With the chain rule, e to the k x differentiates to k times itself.

heading: Differentiating e to the x squared
text: For y = e^(x^2) the chain rule multiplies the exponential by the derivative of the exponent, giving 2x times e to the x squared.

heading: Growth and decay equations
text: When the rate of change is proportional to the amount present, the solution is an exponential. A positive rate constant gives growth and a negative one gives decay.

heading: Half-life of decay
text: In radioactive decay the amount halves after a fixed time. Setting the exponential equal to half the start gives the half-life as the natural logarithm of two divided by the rate.

heading: The natural logarithm
text: The natural logarithm is the inverse of e to the x and can be defined as the area under one over t from one to x. It converts multiplication into addition.

heading: Derivative of the logarithm
text: The derivative of the natural logarithm is one over x. This fills the gap in the power rule, providing the antiderivative of one over x.

heading: Logarithmic differentiation
text: Taking the logarithm of a product before differentiating turns it into a sum. For y = ln(x^2 + 1) the chain rule gives 2x over x squared plus one.

heading: Separable equations
text: A separable differential equation can be rearranged so each variable sits with its own differential. Integrating both sides then gives the solution.

heading: The logistic equation
text: The logistic model adds a ceiling to exponential growth: the rate slows as the population nears its carrying capacity. The solution is an S-shaped curve that levels off.

heading: Powers versus exponentials
text: A power function x to the n and an exponential e to the x grow very differently. For large x the exponential eventually overtakes every power, no matter how large the exponent.
formulas: e^x / x^n -> infinity as x -> infinity

heading: The exponential as a power series
text: The exponential can be written as an infinite sum of powers, each term the previous times x over its index. This series makes clear why e to the x is its own derivative.
formulas: differentiating shifts the series to itself

heading: Hyperbolic functions
text: The hyperbolic sine and cosine are built from exponentials and satisfy an identity like the circular functions but with a minus sign. They describe hanging cables and other exponential combinations.

heading: Derivatives of hyperbolic functions
text: The hyperbolic functions differentiate almost like the trigonometric ones, but without the sign change: the derivative of sinh is cosh and the derivative of cosh is sinh.

heading: Integration by parts
text: Integration by parts reverses the product rule. It trades an integral of u times dv for the simpler boundary term u v minus the integral of v times du.
formulas: integral u dv = u v - integral v du
choose u to simplify when differentiated

heading: Integrating x times e to the x
text: Choosing u = x and dv = e^x dx gives du = dx and v = e^x. Integration by parts yields x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which is x e^x minus e^x.
formulas: integral x e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C

heading: Trigonometric integrals
text: Products of sines and cosines are integrated using Pythagorean identities and, for even powers, the half-angle formulas. The idea is to reshape the integrand into a form ready for substitution.
formulas: use u = sin x or u = cos x for odd powers

heading: Integrating sine squared
text: Using the half-angle formula, the integral of sine squared becomes one half x minus one quarter sine of two x, since the constant and the cosine term integrate directly.
formulas: integral sin^2 x dx = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C

heading: Trigonometric substitution
text: Integrals with square roots of quadratic expressions are simplified by substituting a trigonometric function so a Pythagorean identity removes the root.
formulas: for sqrt(a^2 - x^2) use x = a sin theta
for sqrt(a^2 + x^2) use x = a tan theta
for sqrt(x^2 - a^2) use x = a sec theta

heading: A root simplified by substitution
text: For the integral involving the square root of one minus x squared, substituting x = sin theta turns the root into cosine theta, reducing the integral to one in theta.
formulas: x = sin theta, dx = cos theta d theta

heading: Partial fractions
text: A rational function is split into simpler fractions with linear or quadratic denominators. Each piece integrates to a logarithm or an arctangent.
formulas: integral A/(x - r) dx = A ln|x - r| + C

heading: Splitting a rational function
text: The fraction one over x times (x minus one) splits into minus one over x plus one over (x minus one). Integrating each gives the difference of two logarithms.

heading: Improper integrals
text: An improper integral has an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand. It is defined as a limit of ordinary integrals, and converges only if that limit is finite.
formulas: integral_a^infinity f dx = lim_(b->infinity) integral_a^b f dx
converges if the limit is finite

heading: Convergence of a power integral
text: The integral of one over x squared from one to infinity converges to one, while the integral of one over x diverges. The exponent decides whether the tail area is finite.

heading: Areas and volumes by slices
text: A region or solid is measured by integrating the area of thin slices. For a solid of revolution the slices are disks whose area is pi times the radius squared.

heading: Volume of a cone
text: Revolving the line y = (r/h) x gives disks of that radius. Integrating pi times the radius squared from zero to h yields the cone volume one third pi r squared h.

heading: Length of a curve
text: Arc length adds up tiny hypotenuses along the curve. Each piece is the square root of one plus the slope squared, integrated over the interval.

heading: Length along a curve
text: For a curve whose slope is known, substituting the slope into the arc-length formula gives an integral in x. For the line y = 2x from 0 to 1 the length is the square root of five.

heading: Area of a surface of revolution
text: Spinning a curve about an axis sweeps out a surface. Its area integrates the circumference two pi times the radius against the arc-length element.
formulas: area = integral 2 pi y sqrt(1 + (dy/dx)^2) dx

heading: Probability density
text: A probability density is a nonnegative function whose total integral is one. The probability of a range equals the area under the density over that range.
formulas: P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b p(x) dx

heading: Mean and variance
text: The mean is the integral of x times the density, and the variance measures spread as the integral of the squared deviation. Both are averages computed by integration.

heading: Masses and moments
text: Total mass integrates the density along the object, and the moment integrates distance times density. The center of mass is the moment divided by the total mass.

heading: Center of mass of a rod
text: A uniform rod has its center of mass at the midpoint. Integrating x over the length and dividing by the length confirms the balance point is halfway.
formulas: center of mass = (1/L) integral_0^L x dx

heading: Force, work, and energy
text: Work is the integral of force over the distance moved. When force varies with position, only integration adds up the contributions correctly.
formulas: spring work = integral_0^d k x dx = (1/2) k d^2

heading: Work to stretch a spring
text: A spring force k x grows with stretch, so the work to stretch it a distance d integrates k x, giving one half k d squared. This equals the stored elastic energy.
formulas: work = integral_0^d k x dx = (1/2) k d^2
